name: \( H_{cond} = k A \frac{T_2 - T_1}{l} \)
e: This is Fourier's conduction rate: H equals k A times the temperature drop over thickness l. Bigger k, bigger area, or a thinner wall raises the heat current. The unit of k is watt per metre per kelvin.

name: \( H_{conv} = q A (T_2 - T_1) \)
e: Newton's law of cooling writes the convection rate as q A Delta T. The coefficient q lives in watt per metre squared per kelvin and depends on the fluid motion. You use this only when the fluid itself is moving.

name: \( H_{rad} = e \sigma A T^4 \)
e: Radiated heat current goes as e sigma A T to the fourth. Absolute temperature sits to the fourth power, so a small kelvin change swings the power hard. e is emissivity, 1 for a blackbody.

name: \( \Delta U = Q - W \)
e: First law: the change in internal energy is heat added to the system minus work done by the system. Flip the work sign and you are counting work done on the system instead. Q and W are energies in transit, not stored heat.

name: \( \eta = \frac{W}{Q_H} \)
e: Heat-engine efficiency is work out divided by heat taken from the hot reservoir. Only that fraction of Q_H becomes useful work. The rest leaves as Q_C to the cold side.

name: \( \eta = 1 - \frac{Q_C}{Q_H} \)
content: Heat engine efficiency (in terms of heat)
e: For a cycle, W equals Q_H minus Q_C, so efficiency is also 1 minus the heat dumped over the heat taken. Smaller Q_C at fixed Q_H means a better engine. You can score the engine from the two heats alone.

name: \( \eta_c = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} \)
e: Carnot efficiency is 1 minus T_C over T_H, with both temperatures on an absolute scale. Lower the cold reservoir or raise the hot one and the ceiling climbs. No real engine between those reservoirs can beat this value.
